summary: This unit teaches you to prepare high-level and sensitive written materials in a Jamaican ministry, agency or public body: briefing notes, Cabinet submissions, speeches, answers to questions in Parliament, press material, letters for senior signature and reports. You will learn to write clearly for a senior reader, check facts and figures, handle confidential information securely, work through clearance, meet deadlines and act with integrity.

blocks.p: Senior decision-makers in a public body, such as the Minister, the Permanent Secretary, the Chief Executive Officer or the Cabinet, depend on written material prepared by officers. These documents are **high-level** because they go to or from senior people and shape decisions, and **sensitive** because they may contain confidential policy, personal data, costs not yet announced or matters of public controversy. A mistake can embarrass the Minister, mislead a decision, expose private information or damage public trust.

This unit is for Level 5 supervisors, managers and policy officers who draft for others to sign or present. The work combines good writing, accurate checking, good process (consultation, clearance, version control) and good judgement about confidentiality and honesty.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in your work
rows: Understand the task and the reader
Find out what the senior reader needs to know and decide, and by when.
Write briefing notes
Put the point first, give facts, options and a clear recommendation in one or two pages.
Prepare Cabinet submissions
Use the required headings, consult finance, legal and other agencies, and put the figures right.
Draft speeches, answers to Parliament and press material
Write for the ear, give accurate and concise replies, and prepare lines to take and likely follow-up questions.
Write letters and reports for senior signature
Choose the right tone, include reference, date and signatory, and keep reports factual and impartial.
Protect sensitive information
Classify, limit access, store and send securely, anonymise and respond correctly to a leak or mistake.
Check, clear and deliver
Verify facts, use version control, obtain clearance, manage time and priorities.
Act with integrity
Stay politically neutral, give honest advice and refuse to alter facts to flatter a programme.

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper on briefing notes, Cabinet submissions, speeches, Parliament, letters, reports, security and ethics.
A written paper with short answers (exact terms such as BLUF, annex, redact, clearance, Hansard) and longer answers in which you plan and draft.
Group practicals: a ministerial briefing note with speaking notes, taken through clearance; and a Cabinet submission with a clearance meeting.

blocks.note: For every task, ask first: Who is the reader? What must they know or decide? By when? What is sensitive here?
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Understanding the task, the reader and the rules of the office

blocks.h: Start with the reader and the decision

blocks.p: When you are asked to prepare something for a Minister or a Permanent Secretary, begin by **establishing what the reader needs to know and decide, and by when.** Then find out the format required, the length, who must clear it and any confidentiality marking.

ul: Short on time: the point must come first.
Needs the facts to be **accurate**, because the reader is accountable.
Needs options and a recommendation, not only information.
Needs to know the risks, including public and media reaction.
Needs no surprises.

blocks.p: **BLUF** stands for "**bottom line up front**": state the main point, the decision or the action sought at the start, then give the supporting detail. Many senior readers decide from the first paragraph. A short **summary of the issue and the action sought** at the start lets busy readers grasp the point and decide quickly.

ul: Short sentences and everyday words; **plain language** that the reader can understand the first time.
Active voice: "The ministry will pay all claims by 30 June."
Spell out each abbreviation at first use, or add a list.
Avoid jargon, long chains of clauses and vague words.
Use headings, short paragraphs and tables for figures.

head: Rule
What it means for you
rows: Political neutrality
Public officers give impartial advice and prepare facts and policy material; they do not write party political material, such as a speech for a political rally
Accountability
The Minister answers to Parliament; your work must be accurate and honest so that she can do so
Clearance
Documents go through managers and relevant units for approval before they reach the Minister
Need to know
Confidential material is shared only with those who need it for their work
Records
Final versions and key drafts are filed in the official records system
Access to information
Many documents can be requested by the public under the access to information law, so write as if the public might one day read it

blocks.note: The Cabinet Secretary heads the public service and is secretary to the Cabinet. Cabinet documents follow the Cabinet Office's instructions, which change from time to time. Always check the current format with your Permanent Secretary's office or the Cabinet Office.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **briefing note** is a short document that gives a senior person the key facts on an issue before a meeting or a decision. It is not a history of the matter; it is a tool for deciding or speaking.

head: Heading
What goes in it
rows: Purpose (or action sought)
What the note is for and what the reader must do: decide, note or be ready to speak
Issue
The problem or question in two or three sentences
Background
Only the facts the reader needs: dates, figures, decisions already made
Options
A few realistic options, each with advantages, disadvantages and cost
Recommendation
Your advice, which follows from the analysis, and says exactly what is to be decided
Next steps
Who will do what, by when, once the decision is made
Annexes
Supporting material, such as tables, letters or legal texts, for those who want it
Contact officer
Name and number, in case of questions

blocks.p: A common order for headings is: **purpose, issue, background, options, recommendation.** Whatever order the office uses, keep the point first and the recommendation clear.

ul: Present **a few realistic options**, not every possibility.
For each, give the advantages, disadvantages, costs, risks and time needed.
Say which you recommend and why.
Do not present a weak option only to make the recommended one look good.

blocks.p: A recommendation is sound when it **follows from the analysis and says what is to be decided.** "The Minister is asked to approve Option B, at a cost of J$12,000,000 in this financial year" is a sound recommendation. "More work is needed" is not.

A briefing note on a sensitive subject, such as a new water tariff, should point out the **likely public and media reaction** and the lines the Minister may use. This lets the Minister weigh it and plan how to explain it.

When the Minister needs a one-page update in an hour, write a **short briefing note with the key facts and actions**: what has happened, what is being done, what is not yet known, and what she may be asked. Put the most important point first. Do not wait for a perfect document.

flow: Find out what the reader needs and the deadline
Collect facts and check each figure against its source
Write the purpose and the recommendation first
Fill in issue, background and options briefly
Check numbers and wording; ask a colleague to review
Clear it with your manager and those in the chain
Send it, and keep a record

blocks.p: When the Minister is to meet a group, such as bus operators who are protesting about a licence fee, add: who will attend and what each wants; the Minister's key messages; likely questions and suggested answers; and what the Minister should not say or promise.

If you must explain a complex engineering report in a note for the Minister, **write a plain-language summary and ask the engineers to check it** for accuracy. A summary that changes the meaning is worse than no summary.

A **Cabinet submission** is the document a ministry sends to Cabinet asking it to make a decision on a proposal. Because Cabinet decisions bind the Government and often involve public money, submissions must be complete, accurate and cleared.

head: Section
What it contains
rows: Purpose
The decision sought, in a sentence or two
Background
Why the matter has arisen; what has been decided before
Discussion and options
The analysis, the options considered and the recommended option
Consultations
Which agencies, the Ministry of Finance, legal officers and other bodies were consulted, and what they said
Financial implications
What the proposal will cost, in which years, and how it will be paid for
Legal implications
Whether new legislation or regulations are needed and the legal risks
Risks
What could go wrong and how it will be managed
Communication
How the decision will be announced and explained
Decisions sought
The exact points on which Cabinet is asked to decide
Annexes
Detailed tables, legal texts, consultation responses

blocks.note: Practice and headings vary with the Cabinet Office's current guidelines. Follow the format your ministry's Cabinet liaison unit gives you.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Receive the request and confirm the purpose, the deadline and who is leading
Gather the facts, figures and earlier decisions
Consult finance, legal officers and the agencies affected, and record their comments
Draft the submission, with options and a clear recommendation
Check every figure twice, including totals and years
Circulate the draft for clearance by the director, senior director and Permanent Secretary
Revise, and obtain the Minister's approval
Send to the Cabinet Office by the deadline
File the final version and key drafts in the records system

blocks.p: **Consult before finalising.** If the legal unit has not yet commented and the submission is due in three days, follow up with the legal unit and warn your manager of the risk. Do not send a document forward as though it has been cleared when it has not.

Cost tables must be clear and correct. For example, a programme costing J$180,000,000 for 12,000 people costs J$180,000,000 ÷ 12,000 = **J$15,000** per person. A programme costing J$600,000,000 over three years with equal payments costs J$200,000,000 a year. Present options over the same period in a clear table with totals, and check the sums twice.

head: Option
Year 1 (J$)
Year 2 (J$)
Year 3 (J$)
Total (J$)
rows: A: central office delivery
B: parish-based delivery

blocks.p: Cost per person and weeks to clear a backlog are common checks. A backlog of 3,600 files cleared by a team that closes 240 files a week takes 3,600 ÷ 240 = **15 weeks**.

An **annex** is a section at the end that holds detailed supporting material, such as tables or legal texts. Keep the main text short and put detail in annexes. Spell out each abbreviation at first use.

ul: Write for the **ear**: short sentences, clear structure, simple words, a strong opening and close.
Check every fact and figure with the programme's records before sending.
Allow time: a speaker talks at about 130 words a minute. An 8-minute speech is about 8 × 130 = **1,040** words.
Include pauses and local references.
Do not write party political material (such as a speech for a party rally). Explain that it is outside your role.
Do not announce a decision that has not yet been made or approved.

blocks.p: Members of the House of Representatives and Senators may table questions to Ministers. The officer's task is to prepare an **accurate, concise draft reply**, with notes for the Minister.

flow: Note the exact wording of the question and the date it must be answered
Identify what is asked and what is not
Collect the facts from the unit and check them
Draft a short, direct and accurate reply
Prepare notes: background, figures and likely follow-up questions
Clear it through the chain
Send to the Minister's office in good time

blocks.p: After the answer, a Member may ask a **supplementary question**. Officers prepare notes on likely follow-up questions so that the Minister is ready. The official record of debates in Parliament is **Hansard**.

blocks.note: A wrong statement made to Parliament is serious. If you discover an error after a draft has gone forward, tell your manager at once so that it can be corrected.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Item
What it is
rows: Press release
A short statement to the media on an announcement, with the main facts first
Lines to take
Agreed short answers to likely questions, for the speakers
Embargo
A rule that the information must not be published before a stated time (for example "embargoed until 10:00 a.m. Thursday")
Questions and answers
A fuller set of likely questions with answers
Holding statement
A short statement used while the facts are being checked

blocks.p: Before a press conference on a sensitive matter, such as a delayed project, prepare **lines to take**, agree them with the Minister's office and brief everyone who may speak. If different officers give different answers, the story becomes the inconsistency.

When describing a community in a report or release, do so **fairly and factually, avoiding stereotypes and blame.** Language that blames a group for a social problem damages trust and may be unfair or untrue.

sections.title: Letters and reports for senior signature

blocks.h: Letters for the Permanent Secretary or Minister

ul: Include the **file reference, the date and the signatory's title.**
Open with the point, then give reasons and next steps.
Use a courteous, human tone: avoid stiff phrases such as "We regret that we cannot approve" without explanation.
Give clear next steps: what the person can do and by when.
Have a manager and senior officers clear it before it goes up for signature.

head: Stiff and unclear
Better
rows: "We have considered your application and regret that we cannot approve it."
"We cannot approve your application because the land title is missing. If you send a copy by 30 June, we will review it again."

blocks.p: When writing to a family in grief, such as the family of an officer who died in an accident at work, the letter must be **sincere, respectful and clear about support and next steps.** When the ministry has made an error, such as a delayed pension, state plainly that the error was the ministry's, apologise, say what is being done and by when, and give a contact.

blocks.h: Reports for senior officers and boards

ul: Begin with an **executive summary** that gives the main findings, their effects and the recommendations.
Stick to **facts and evidence**; keep opinion out of an investigation report.
Be fair to all parties; give each a fair account.
Remove or **anonymise** personal details not needed for the purpose: for example, the names, addresses and medical details of 40 clients.
Keep a clear structure: purpose, method, findings, conclusions, recommendations.
Ask a colleague to check facts, figures and wording before it goes up.

blocks.p: If a director asks you to leave a finding out of a draft report because it will embarrass the Minister, **explain that impartial advice includes such findings.** Senior officers need the full picture to decide well. You may help to present the finding fairly and constructively, but not remove it.

A **security classification** is the grading given to a document, such as "confidential" or "secret". It tells people how to handle it. The **need to know** principle means only people who need the information for their work should see it. Marking a document confidential does not make it safe unless it is also handled correctly.

head: Stage
What to do
rows: Drafting
Mark the draft with its classification and a version number; keep it off shared or public drives
Storing
Lock paper copies away; use password-protected folders; follow a **clear-desk rule**
Copying
Copy only what is needed, and keep a record of numbered copies
Sending
Use the approved secure system, marked confidential; do not use personal email or messaging apps
Discussing
Not in corridors, taxis or on speakerphone; not with those who do not need to know
Disposing
Shred paper; securely delete files you no longer need, according to records rules

blocks.p: Where several officers edit a document, use **version control:** numbered drafts, dates, a change log and one person responsible for the master copy. Without it, people edit old versions, changes are lost and mistakes reach the Minister. Name files clearly: "Cabinet note, water tanks, v3, 14 March, cleared by Director".

Suppose you realise that you have emailed a confidential draft to the wrong outside address. **Report it to your manager at once, as policy requires.** Do not hope that nobody will notice and do not try to hide it. Early reporting lets the agency ask the recipient to delete the message and reduces harm.

flow: Stop: do not send any more copies
Report immediately to your manager and the security or records officer
Say exactly what was sent, to whom and when
Follow instructions to recall or delete and to inform those affected
Write a short record of what happened
Learn: change the habit or system that allowed the mistake

blocks.h: Access to information and personal data

ul: Many documents can be requested under the **access to information law**, whose purpose is to give the public access to official documents, with exceptions. Write on the assumption that internal memos and reports could one day be seen.
A response to a request may release a document with **sensitive parts removed**. To **redact** is to black out or remove the sensitive parts before release.
The **data protection law** controls how personal information is used and kept. Use only what the purpose needs and protect it.
Do not decide on your own what is to be released. Follow the agency's procedure and the advice of the legal unit or the access to information officer.

blocks.p: Respect embargoes: information marked "embargoed until 10:00 a.m. Thursday" must not be published before that time. The official government publication in which new laws, regulations and official notices are published is the **Jamaica Gazette**.

**Clearance** means obtaining each required senior officer's approval of a document before it goes forward. Normally the officer's manager and the senior officers in the chain clear a sensitive letter before it reaches the Minister for signature.

head: Check
Questions to ask
rows: Accuracy
Is every fact and figure verified against a source? Have I checked totals and units?
Clarity
Can the reader understand it the first time? Are abbreviations explained?
Fitness for purpose
Does it meet the request, format and length? Does it answer the reader's question?
Completeness
Have I included options, risks and consultation?
Consistency
Do names, dates and figures agree throughout, and with earlier documents?
Sensitivity
Is it correctly marked, and are private details removed?
Tone
Is it neutral, respectful and fair?

blocks.p: The best review question is: **Is it accurate, clear and fit for its purpose?** Where possible, ask a colleague to check facts, figures and wording; a fresh reader catches what the writer cannot.

When a director returns your draft with many changes, **study the changes and ask about unclear points.** You will learn the preferred style and the reasons, and your next draft will improve. Do not take it personally, and do not ignore the changes.

Suppose you have two tasks due today: an urgent brief for the Minister's 3:00 p.m. meeting and a routine monthly report. Do the **urgent brief first and agree a new time for the report.** Tell the person waiting for the report early, not after the deadline.
When a sensitive paper is due on Thursday at noon and four units must be consulted, plan backwards from the deadline:

flow: Confirm the exact deadline and what is wanted
List the units to be consulted and contact each at once, giving a date for comment
Draft while the comments come in
Allow time for clearance and final checks
Warn the manager early if any unit is late
Keep a log of who said what and when

blocks.note: You must never change figures or facts so that a programme looks more successful than it is. If a senior officer, or the Minister's office, asks you to do so, **decline and raise it through proper channels:** your manager, the Permanent Secretary or the agency's integrity channel. Honest advice protects the Minister as well as the public.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Give impartial, evidence-based advice.
Never mislead Parliament, the Cabinet or the public.
Report pressure to alter the facts.
Keep to the Code of Conduct and the agency's rules.
Do not use confidential information for private gain or share it with the media. Do not seek the media's comment on a draft Cabinet document.

blocks.p: After a sensitive submission is approved, the final version and key drafts should be **filed in the official records system.** This keeps the record clear and allows later audit, inquiry or access requests.

ul: establish what a senior reader needs to know and decide, and by when.

prepare a Cabinet submission with the usual headings, consult finance, legal and agencies, and check the figures.

write a speech for the ear and estimate its length at 130 words a minute.

terms: Briefing note
A short document giving a senior person the key facts on an issue before a meeting or decision.
BLUF
Bottom line up front: put the main point first.
Cabinet submission
A ministry's document asking Cabinet to make a decision.
Annex
A section at the end holding detailed supporting material.
Plain language
Writing the reader can understand the first time.
Clearance
Obtaining each required senior officer's approval before a document goes forward.
Need to know
The rule that only people who need information for their work may see it.
Security classification
The grading given to a document, such as confidential or secret.
Redact
To black out or remove sensitive parts of a document before release.
Version control
Numbered drafts, dates and a change log to avoid confusion among editors.
Lines to take
Agreed short answers to likely questions, for speakers.
Embargo
A rule that information must not be published before a stated time.
Supplementary question
An extra question that may follow the Minister's answer to the main question.
Hansard
The official written record of debates in Parliament.
Jamaica Gazette
The official publication of new laws, regulations and official notices.
Cabinet Secretary
The head of the public service, who is also secretary to the Cabinet.
Executive summary
A short section at the start of a report giving the main findings and recommendations.
Impartial advice
Advice based on evidence, which includes unwelcome findings.

c1.title: A Cabinet submission on rural water tanks
c1.text: A ministry in Kingston wants Cabinet to approve a three-year programme to supply water tanks to 2,400 households in drought-prone parishes at a total cost of J$360,000,000. Mr Andre Campbell, a senior policy officer, is drafting the submission. The Ministry of Finance and the legal unit have not yet commented, and the Cabinet Office deadline is in four days. A colleague suggests sending the draft to a newspaper reporter 'to test public reaction'.

c2.title: A question about road repairs in Parliament
c2.text: A Member of Parliament has tabled a question asking how many kilometres of road were repaired in St Elizabeth last year. The programme unit reports 140 km. The works agency's records show 128 km. Ms Beverley Thompson, a ministry officer, must prepare the draft reply and notes for the Minister. The Minister's office wants it by Wednesday morning.

c3.title: A speech for a community centre opening
c3.text: The Minister will open a community centre in Hanover and speak for 8 minutes. Mr Dwight Reid has been asked to draft the speech. A senior colleague asks him to add praise of the Government's party and to announce a new grant that Cabinet has not yet approved. The Minister speaks at about 130 words a minute.

c4.title: A sensitive report on a fraud inquiry
c4.text: Mrs Janice Morgan has written a draft report to the Permanent Secretary on a fraud inquiry at a regional office. It names three staff and includes the medical details of one of them. Four officers have edited it by email and now each has a different version. Mrs Morgan realises that she has sent the draft to a wrong outside email address.

c5.title: A request for a report and a letter for signature
c5.text: A citizen has asked the ministry for a copy of an internal review report under the access to information law. The report contains advice to Cabinet and the personal details of 15 clients. Mr Roy Gray must draft the letter of reply for the Permanent Secretary's signature. The director returns his first draft with many changes.

questions.q: Which step must come before Mr Campbell finalises the submission?
o: Consulting finance and legal officers and recording their comments
Sending the draft to the Minister's office to be signed at once
Asking a newspaper to comment on the programme and its costs
Asking each affected agency to approve the final wording
questions.why: Cabinet submissions need the comments of finance and legal officers on costs and law, so that Cabinet can decide on a complete and sound proposal.

questions.q: The legal unit has not commented and the deadline is in four days. What should Mr Campbell do?
o: Send the submission without the legal comments, to meet the deadline
Follow up with the legal unit and warn his manager of the risk
Remove the section on legal implications until the unit replies
Wait for the legal unit to reply, however late the reply may be
questions.why: Chasing the unit and informing the manager keeps the work on time and honest. A submission must not be presented as cleared when it is not.

questions.q: What is the cost per household of the programme?
questions.why: J$360,000,000 ÷ 2,400 = J$150,000 per household. Check figures twice before they go to Cabinet.

questions.q: A colleague suggests sending the draft to a reporter 'to test public reaction'. What should Mr Campbell do?
o: Agree, but remove the cost figures from the draft before sending it
Agree, if the reporter first promises not to publish any of it
Decline, unless the Permanent Secretary is told about it afterwards
Decline, since a draft Cabinet document is confidential
questions.why: A draft Cabinet submission is confidential. Sharing it with the media is not part of preparing a submission, and it could damage the decision and breach the rules.

questions.q: The programme unit reports 140 km and the works agency 128 km. What should Ms Thompson do?
o: Find the reason for the difference and use the verified figure
Use the larger figure, because it is the more favourable one
Use the smaller figure, because it is the safer one to give
Give both figures and let the Minister choose between them
questions.why: An answer to Parliament must be accurate. Check the sources and definitions and explain the verified figure. Choosing a figure for convenience may mislead.

questions.q: Which should accompany the draft reply to the Minister?
o: A list of every road repaired in the parish since the year 2010
Notes on background, figures and likely follow-up questions
A copy of the works agency's full annual report for last year
The names of the officers who collected the repair data
questions.why: The Minister may face supplementary questions, so she needs short notes to answer them with confidence.

questions.q: What is the best style for the draft reply itself?
o: Long and detailed, covering the whole of the roads programme
General in tone, so as to avoid any commitment on figures
Short, direct and accurate, answering exactly what was asked
Persuasive, with praise for the ministry's work on the roads
questions.why: A reply should answer the question that was asked, briefly and accurately. Extra material belongs in the notes.

questions.q: Ms Thompson finds a small error in a draft that has already gone to the director. What should she do?
o: Wait to see whether anyone else notices the error first
Change the final version quietly without telling anyone
Mention it only if the Minister happens to ask about it
Tell her manager at once so that it can be corrected
questions.why: Errors should be reported and corrected early, especially for Parliament. Hiding them risks misleading the House.

questions.q: About how many words should the 8-minute speech contain?
o: About 1,040
About 800
About 1,300
About 1,560
questions.why: 8 × 130 = 1,040 words. Allow a little less for pauses and applause.

questions.q: The colleague asks Mr Reid to add praise of the Government's party. What should he do?
o: Add it, but keep the praise to a single short sentence
Explain that party political material is outside his role
Add it, since the speech belongs to the Minister in the end
Add it only if the Minister's office asks for it in writing
questions.why: Public officers give impartial advice and do not write party political material. The Minister's office may deal with party matters separately.

questions.q: The colleague wants the speech to announce a grant that Cabinet has not approved. What should Mr Reid do?
o: Include it, with the words 'subject to approval' in the text
Include it, since Cabinet is expected to approve it very soon
Leave it out and tell his manager that it is not yet approved
Put it in the speaking notes but leave it out of the speech
questions.why: Announcing an unapproved decision could mislead the public and embarrass the Minister. Raise the matter with the manager.

questions.q: The Minister decides to speak from brief points instead of a full text. What should Mr Reid prepare?
o: A longer version of the speech with all the background included
A briefing note on the history of the community centre project
A list of questions that the audience is likely to ask her
Speaking notes: key points, facts and figures on one or two pages
questions.why: Speaking notes give short points to guide what to say. The key facts must still be checked, and the points should follow the speech's structure.

questions.q: Mrs Morgan's draft includes the medical details of one officer. What should she do?
o: Remove them unless they are needed for the report's purpose
Keep them, to show that the inquiry was done thoroughly
Keep them, but mark that page of the report confidential
Move them to an annex at the end, without any heading
questions.why: Personal details not needed for the purpose should be removed or anonymised, in line with the data protection law.

questions.q: Four officers have edited the report and each has a different version. What is the best remedy?
o: Ask everyone to send their changes straight to the Permanent Secretary
Version control, with numbered drafts, dates and a master copy
Ask each officer to edit only the page that was assigned to them
Merge the changes from memory at the final meeting of the officers
questions.why: Version control avoids lost changes and confusion, and one person keeps the master copy.

questions.q: She realises that she has sent the draft to a wrong outside address. What should she do first?
o: Send a second email asking the recipient to ignore the first one
Wait to see whether the recipient replies before telling anyone
Report it to her manager at once, as the policy requires
Tell only the three officers who are named in the report
questions.why: Early reporting lets the agency act quickly to limit harm. Hiding the mistake makes it worse.

questions.q: Which style is best for the findings in an investigation report?
o: Strong language, to show that the fraud is serious
The investigator's views on the officers' general characters
Rumours heard during the inquiry, clearly marked as rumours
Facts and evidence, with opinion kept out
questions.why: An investigation report must be fair and based on evidence. Opinion and rumour could be unfair and may harm the process.

questions.q: The report has advice to Cabinet and the personal details of 15 clients. How should the ministry respond to the request?
o: Follow the procedure with legal advice, and redact sensitive parts
Refuse the request in full, because the report is an internal one
Release the full report, because the law favours openness
Decide in the writer's own office and tell the legal unit afterwards
questions.why: The access to information law allows release with exceptions. The officer follows the procedure and takes advice, and does not decide alone.

questions.q: What does it mean to redact a document?
o: To translate the document into plain language for readers
To black out or remove sensitive parts before release
To file the document in the official records system
To mark the document with a security classification
questions.why: Redaction protects personal data and exempt material while allowing the rest to be released.

questions.q: Which is the best tone for the letter of reply to the citizen?
o: Formal and brief, with no explanation of the decision made
Defensive, in order to protect the ministry's position
Clear, courteous and helpful, with reasons and next steps
Detailed and legal, in order to cover every possible risk
questions.why: A good reply is clear and respectful, says what is released and what is not and why, and tells the citizen what to do next.

questions.q: Why should Mr Gray take special care with the part of the report that contains advice to Cabinet?
o: It is the longest part and the most difficult to summarise
The citizen has already seen it in the media
Advice to Cabinet may always be freely released to the public
Cabinet advice may be exempt, so seek legal advice first
questions.why: Cabinet's deliberations are protected by confidentiality rules and exemptions. The officer must take advice and follow the procedure, not decide alone.
